Euler Equations Related
to the Generalized Neveu–Schwarz Algebra

Dafeng ZUO †‡
Abstract

In this paper, we study supersymmetric or bi-superhamiltonian Euler equations related to the generalized Neveu–Schwarz algebra. As an application, we obtain several supersymmetric or bi-superhamiltonian generalizations of some well-known integrable systems including the coupled KdV equation, the 2-component Camassa–Holm equation and the 2-component Hunter–Saxton equation. To our knowledge, most of them are new.

supersymmetric; bi-superhamiltonian; Euler equations; generalized Neveu–Schwarz algebra

1 Introduction

For a classical rigid body with a fixed point, the configuration space is the group SO⁡(3){\rm SO}(3) of rotations of three-dimensional Euclidean space. In 1765, L. Euler proposed the equations of motion of the rigid body describing as geodesics in SO⁡(3){\rm SO}(3), where SO⁡(3){\rm SO}(3) is provided with a left-invariant metric. In essence, the Euler theory of a rigid theory is fully described by this invariance.

Let GG be an arbitrary (possibly infinite-dimensional) Lie group and 𝒢\mathcal{G} the corresponding Lie algebra and 𝒢∗\mathcal{G}^{*} the dual of 𝒢\mathcal{G}. V.I. Arnold in [3] suggested a general framework for Euler equations on GG, which can be regarded as a configuration space of some physical systems. In this framework Euler equations describe geodesic flows w.r.t. suitable one-side invariant Riemannian metrics on GG and can be given to a variety of conservative dynamical systems in mathematical physics, for instance, see [2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 24, 25, 28, 30, 32, 33, 35, 37, 39] and references therein.

Since V. Ovsienko and B. Khesin in [35] interpreted the Kuper–KdV equation [23] as a geodesic flow equation on the superconformal group w.r.t. an L2L^{2}-type metric, it has been attracted a lot of interest in studying super (fermionic or supersymmetric) anologue of Arnold’s approach, which has some different characteristic flavors, for instance [2, 11, 16, 23, 24, 25, 36, 38].

In this paper, we are interested in Euler equations related to the N=1N=1 generalized Neveu–Schwarz (GNS in brief) algebra 𝒢\mathcal{G}, which was introduced by P. Marcel, V. Ovsienko and C. Roger in [29] as a generalization of the N=1N=1 Neveu–Schwarz algebra and the extended Virasoro algebra. In [16], P. Guha and P.J. Ovler have studied the Euler equations related to the GNS algebra 𝒢\mathcal{G} and obtained fermionic versions of the 2-component Camassa–Holm equation and the Ito equation in some special metrics. Our motivations are twofold. One is to study the Euler equation related to 𝒢\mathcal{G} for a more general metric Mc1,c2,c3,c4,c5,c6M_{c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4},c_{5},c_{6}} in (2.1) with six-parameters given by

⟨F^,G^⟩=∫S1(c1​f​g+c2​fx​gx+c3​ϕ​∂−1χ+c4​ϕx​χ+c5​a​b+c6​α​∂−1β)​𝑑x+σ→⋅τ→,\displaystyle\langle\hat{F},\hat{G}\rangle=\int_{S^{1}}\big(c_{1}fg+c_{2}f_{x}g_{x}+c_{3}\phi\partial^{-1}\chi+c_{4}\phi_{x}\chi+c_{5}ab+c_{6}\alpha\partial^{-1}\beta\big)dx+\vec{\sigma}\cdot\vec{\tau},

which can be regarded as a super-version of Sobolev-metrics in the super space. The other is to study the condition under which Euler equations are supersymmetric or bi-superhamiltonian. Our main results is to show that

As a byproduct, we obtain some supersymmetric or bi-superhamiltonian generalizations of some well-known integrable systems including the coupled KdV equation, the 2-component Camassa–Holm equation and the 2-component Hunter–Saxton equation.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we calculate the Euler equation on 𝒢reg∗\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*} and discuss their Hamiltonian properties. In Section 3, we study bi-superhamiltonian Euler equations. Section 4 is devoted to describe supersymmetric Euler equations, also including a class of both supersymmetric and bi-superhamiltonian Euler equations. A few concluding remarks are given in the last section.

2 Euler equations related to the GNS algebra

To be self-contained, let us recall the Anorld’s approach [4, 20, 21]. Let GG be an arbitrary Lie group and 𝒢\mathcal{G} the corresponding Lie algebra and 𝒢∗\mathcal{G}^{*} the dual of 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Firstly let us fix a energy quadratic form E⁡(v)=12​⟨v,𝒜​v⟩∗E(v)=\frac{1}{2}\langle v,\mathcal{A}v\rangle^{*} on 𝒢\mathcal{G} and consider right translations of this quadratic form on 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Then the energy quadratic form defines a right-invariant Riemannian metric on GG. The geodesic flow on GG w.r.t. this energy metric represents the extremals of the least action principle, i.e., the actual motions of our physical system. For a rigid body, one has to consider left translations. We next identify 𝒢\mathcal{G} and its dual 𝒢∗\mathcal{G}^{*} with the help of E⁡(⋅)E(\cdot). This identification 𝒜:𝒢→𝒢∗\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{G}\to\mathcal{G}^{*}, called an inertia operator, allows us to rewrite the Euler equation on 𝒢∗\mathcal{G}^{*}. It turns out that the Euler equation on 𝒢∗\mathcal{G}^{*} is Hamiltonian w.r.t. a canonical Lie–Poisson structure on 𝒢∗\mathcal{G}^{*}. Notice that in some cases it turns out to be not only Hamiltonian, but also bihamiltonian. Moreover, the corresponding Hamiltonian function is −E⁡(m)=−12​⟨𝒜−1​m,m⟩∗-E(m)=-\frac{1}{2}\langle\mathcal{A}^{-1}m,m\rangle^{*} lifted from the Lie algebra 𝒢\mathcal{G} to its dual space 𝒢∗\mathcal{G}^{*}, where m=𝒜​v∈𝒢∗m=\mathcal{A}v\in\mathcal{G}^{*}.

Definition 2.1 ([4, 20]).

The Euler equation on 𝒢∗\mathcal{G}^{*}, corresponding to the right-invariant metric −E⁡(m)=−12​⟨𝒜−1​m,m⟩∗-E(m)=-\frac{1}{2}\langle\mathcal{A}^{-1}m,m\rangle^{*} on GG, is given by the following explicit formula

d​md​t=−ad𝒜−1​m∗​m,\displaystyle\frac{dm}{dt}=-{\rm ad}^{*}_{\mathcal{A}^{-1}m}m,

as an evolution of a point m∈𝒢∗m\in\mathcal{G}^{*}.

Let us remark that the system (2.3) has been obtained in [16] with minor typos. But they didn’t discuss the condition under which the Euler equation (2.3) is supersymmetric or bi-superhamiltonian.

According to Definition 2.1, the Euler equation (2.3) has a natural Hamiltonian description [4, 20, 21]. Let Fi:𝒢∗→ℝF_{i}:\mathcal{G}^{*}\to\mathbb{R}, i=1,2i=1,2, be two arbitrary smooth functionals. The dual space 𝒢∗\mathcal{G}^{*} carries a canonical Lie–Poisson bracket

{F1,F2}2​(U^)=⟨U^,[δ​F1δ​U^,δ​F2δ​U^]⟩∗,\displaystyle\{F_{1},F_{2}\}_{2}(\hat{U})=\left\langle\hat{U},\left[\frac{\delta F_{1}}{\delta\hat{U}},\frac{\delta F_{2}}{\delta\hat{U}}\right]\right\rangle^{*},

where U^∈𝒢∗\hat{U}\in\mathcal{G}^{*} and δ​Fiδ​U^=(δ​Fiδ​u,δ​Fiδ​ψ,δ​Fiδ​v,δ​Fiδ​γ,δ​Fiδ​ς→)∈𝒢,i=1,2\frac{\delta F_{i}}{\delta\hat{U}}=\big(\frac{\delta F_{i}}{\delta u},\frac{\delta F_{i}}{\delta\psi},\frac{\delta F_{i}}{\delta v},\frac{\delta F_{i}}{\delta\gamma},\frac{\delta F_{i}}{\delta\vec{\varsigma}}\big)\in\mathcal{G},i=1,2. The induced superhamiltonian operator is given by

𝒥2=(ς1∂3−u∂−∂u−ψ∂−12∂ψ,−ς2∂2−v∂−γ∂+12∂γ−∂ψ−12ψ∂12u−ς1∂2−12γ∂12v+ς2∂ς2∂2−∂v−12∂γ−2ς3∂0−∂γ+12γ∂12v−ς2∂02​ς3).\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{2}=\left(\begin{matrix}\varsigma_{1}\partial^{3}-u\partial-\partial u&-\psi\partial-\frac{1}{2}\partial\psi,&-\varsigma_{2}\partial^{2}-v\partial&-\gamma\partial+\frac{1}{2}\partial\gamma\\ -\partial\psi-\frac{1}{2}\psi\partial&\frac{1}{2}u-\varsigma_{1}\partial^{2}&-\frac{1}{2}\gamma\partial&\frac{1}{2}v+\varsigma_{2}\partial\\ \varsigma_{2}\partial^{2}-\partial v&-\frac{1}{2}\partial\gamma&-2\varsigma_{3}\partial&0\\ -\partial\gamma+\frac{1}{2}\gamma\partial&\frac{1}{2}v-\varsigma_{2}\partial&0&2\varsigma_{3}\end{matrix}\right). (2.4)
Proposition 2.4.

The Euler equation (2.3) could be written as

dd​t​(u,ψ,v,γ)T=𝒥2​(δ​H1δ​u,δ​H1δ​ψ,δ​H1δ​v,δ​H1δ​γ)T\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}(u,\psi,v,\gamma)^{\rm T}=\mathcal{J}_{2}\left(\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta u},\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta\psi},\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta v},\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta\gamma}\right)^{\rm T} (2.5)

with the Hamiltonian H1=12​∫S1(u​f+ψ​ϕ+v​a+γ​α)​𝑑xH_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{S^{1}}(uf+\psi\phi+va+\gamma\alpha)dx, where (⋅)T(\cdot)^{\rm T} means the transpose of vectors.

Proof.

Indeed, for a functional F⁡[u,ψ,v,γ]F[u,\psi,v,\gamma], the variational derivatives δ​Fδ​u\frac{\delta F}{\delta u}, δ​Fδ​ψ\frac{\delta F}{\delta\psi}, δ​Fδ​v\frac{\delta F}{\delta v} and δ​Fδ​γ\frac{\delta F}{\delta\gamma} are defined by

dd​ϵ∣ϵ=0​F​[u+ϵ​δ​u,ψ+ϵ​δ​ψ,v+ϵ​δ​v,γ+ϵ​δ​γ]\displaystyle\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\mid_{\epsilon=0}F[u+\epsilon\delta u,\psi+\epsilon\delta\psi,v+\epsilon\delta v,\gamma+\epsilon\delta\gamma]
=∫(δ​u​δ​Fδ​u+δ​ψ​δ​Fδ​ψ+δ​v​δ​Fδ​v+δ​γ​δ​Fδ​γ)​𝑑x.\displaystyle\qquad{}=\int\left(\delta u\frac{\delta F}{\delta u}+\delta\psi\frac{\delta F}{\delta\psi}+\delta v\frac{\delta F}{\delta v}+\delta\gamma\frac{\delta F}{\delta\gamma}\right)dx. (2.6)

By using (2.6), we have

δ​H1δ​f=Λ⁡(f),δ​H1δ​ϕ=−Θ⁡(ϕ),δ​H1δ​a=v,δ​H1δ​α=−γ.\displaystyle\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta f}=\Lambda(f),\qquad\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta\phi}=-\Theta(\phi),\qquad\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta a}=v,\qquad\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta\alpha}=-\gamma.

It follows from the definition of uu, ψ\psi and γ\gamma that

δ​H1δ​u=Λ−1​δ​H1δ​u=f,δ​H1δ​ψ=−Θ−1​δ​H1δ​ϕ=ϕ,\displaystyle\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta u}=\Lambda^{-1}\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta u}=f,\qquad\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta\psi}=-\Theta^{-1}\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta\phi}=\phi,
δ​H1δ​v=a,δ​H1δ​γ=−∂δ​H1δ​α=α.\displaystyle\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta v}=a,\qquad\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta\gamma}=-\partial\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta\alpha}=\alpha. (2.7)

Hence, (2.5) could be easily verified by using (2.4) and (2.7). ∎

3 Bihamiltonian Euler equations on 𝓖𝐫𝐞𝐠∗\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*}}

Unless otherwise stated, in the following we use “(bi)hamiltonian” to denote “(bi)-superhamiltonian”. In this section we want to study bihamiltonian Euler equations on 𝒢reg∗\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*} w.r.t. the metric Mc1,c2,14​c1,c2,c5,−c5M_{c_{1},c_{2},\frac{1}{4}c_{1},c_{2},c_{5},-c_{5}} and propose some new bihamiltonian and fermionic extensions of well-known integrable systems including coupled the KdV equation, the 2-CH equation and the 2-HS equation.

3.1 The frozen Lie–Poisson bracket on 𝓖𝐫𝐞𝐠∗\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*}}

For the purpose of discussing possible bihamiltonian Euler equations, we introduce a frozen Lie–Poisson bracket on 𝒢reg∗\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*} defined by

{F1,F2}1​(U^)=⟨U^0,[δ​F1δ​U^,δ​F2δ​U^]⟩∗,\displaystyle\{F_{1},F_{2}\}_{1}(\hat{U})=\left\langle\hat{U}_{0},\left[\frac{\delta F_{1}}{\delta\hat{U}},\frac{\delta F_{2}}{\delta\hat{U}}\right]\right\rangle^{*},

for a fixed point U^0∈𝒢∗\hat{U}_{0}\in{\mathcal{G}}^{*}. The corresponding Hamiltonian equation is given by

d​U^d​t=−adδ​H2δ​U^∗​U^0\displaystyle\frac{d\hat{U}}{dt}=-{\rm ad}^{*}_{\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\hat{U}}}\hat{U}_{0} (3.1)

for a functional H2:𝒢reg∗→ℝH_{2}:{\mathcal{G}^{*}_{\rm reg}}\to\mathbb{R}. If we could find a functional H2H_{2} and a suitable point U^0∈𝒢reg∗\hat{U}_{0}\in\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*} such that the system (3.1) coincides with (2.3). This means that the Euler equation (2.3) is bihamiltonian and could be written as

dd​t​(u,ψ,v,γ)T=𝒥1​(δ​H2δ​u,δ​H2δ​ψ,δ​H2δ​v,δ​H2δ​γ)T=𝒥2​(δ​H1δ​u,δ​H1δ​ψ,δ​H1δ​v,δ​H1δ​γ)T\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}(u,\psi,v,\gamma)^{\rm T}=\mathcal{J}_{1}\left(\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta u},\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\psi},\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta v},\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\gamma}\right)^{\rm T}=\mathcal{J}_{2}\left(\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta u},\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta\psi},\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta v},\frac{\delta H_{1}}{\delta\gamma}\right)^{\rm T}

with Hamiltonian operators 𝒥2\mathcal{J}_{2} in (2.4) and 𝒥1=𝒥2|U^=U^0\mathcal{J}_{1}=\mathcal{J}_{2}|_{\hat{U}=\hat{U}_{0}}. Moreover, according to Proposition 5.3 in [20], {,}1\{~,~\}_{1} and {,}2\{~,~\}_{2} are compatible for every freezing point U^0\hat{U}_{0}.

3.2 Bihamiltonian Euler equations on 𝓖𝐫𝐞𝐠∗\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*}} w.r.t. 𝑴𝒄𝟏,𝒄𝟐,𝟏𝟒​𝒄𝟏,𝒄𝟐,𝒄𝟓,−𝒄𝟓\boldsymbol{M_{c_{1},c_{2},\frac{1}{4}c_{1},c_{2},c_{5},-c_{5}}}

In this case, we have

c1=4​c3,c2=c4,c6=−c5.\displaystyle c_{1}=4\,c_{3},\qquad c_{2}=c_{4},\qquad c_{6}=-c_{5}.

By setting ϕ=ηx\phi=\eta_{x} and α=μx\alpha=\mu_{x}, then

u=Λ⁡(f)=c1​f−c2​fx​x,ψ=Π⁡(η)=c2​ηx​x−14​c1​η,v=c5​a,γ=−c5​μ\displaystyle u=\Lambda(f)=c_{1}f-c_{2}f_{xx},\qquad\psi=\Pi(\eta)=c_{2}\eta_{xx}-\frac{1}{4}c_{1}\eta,\qquad v=c_{5}a,\qquad\gamma=-c_{5}\mu (3.2)

and the Euler equation becomes

ut=ς1​fx​x​x−ς2​ax​x−2​u​fx−ux​f−32​ψ​ηx​x−12​ψx​ηx−v​ax−12​γ​μx​x,\displaystyle u_{t}=\varsigma_{1}f_{xxx}-\varsigma_{2}a_{xx}-2uf_{x}-u_{x}f-\frac{3}{2}\psi\eta_{xx}-\frac{1}{2}\psi_{x}\eta_{x}-va_{x}-\frac{1}{2}\gamma\mu_{xx},
ψt=12​u​ηx−ς1​ηx​x​x+ς2​μx​x−32​fx​ψ−f​ψx+12​(v​μ)x,\displaystyle\psi_{t}=\frac{1}{2}u\eta_{x}-{\varsigma}_{1}\eta_{xxx}+{\varsigma}_{2}\mu_{xx}-\frac{3}{2}f_{x}\psi-f\psi_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(v\mu)_{x},
vt=ς2​fx​x−2​ς3​ax−(v​f)x−12​(γ​ηx)x,\displaystyle v_{t}=\varsigma_{2}f_{xx}-2\varsigma_{3}a_{x}-(vf)_{x}-\frac{1}{2}(\gamma\eta_{x})_{x}, (3.3)
γt=12​v​ηx−γx​f−12​γ​fx−ς2​ηx​x+2​ς3​μx.\displaystyle\gamma_{t}=\frac{1}{2}v\eta_{x}-\gamma_{x}f-\frac{1}{2}\gamma f_{x}-\varsigma_{2}\eta_{xx}+2\varsigma_{3}\mu_{x}.

We are now in a position to state our main theorem.

Theorem 3.1.

The system (3.3) is bihamiltonian on 𝒢reg∗\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*} with a freezing point U^0=(c12​d​x2,0𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸\hat{U}_{0}=\big(\frac{c_{1}}{2}dx^{2},0, 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁0,0,(c2,0,c52))∈𝒢reg∗0,0,\big(c_{2},0,\frac{c_{5}}{2}\big)\big)\in\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*} and a Hamiltionian functional

H2=∫S1(−ς12​f​fx​x+c12​f3−c24​f2​fx​x−c22​f​ηx​ηx​x−3​c18​f​η​ηx+ς12​η​ηx​xCLOSE\displaystyle H_{2}=\int_{S^{1}}\left({-}\frac{\varsigma_{1}}{2}ff_{xx}+\frac{c_{1}}{2}f^{3}-\frac{c_{2}}{4}f^{2}f_{xx}-\frac{c_{2}}{2}f\eta_{x}\eta_{xx}-\frac{3c_{1}}{8}f\eta\eta_{x}+\frac{\varsigma_{1}}{2}\eta\eta_{xx}\right.
OPEN−ς2​a​fx+12​a​v​f+ς3​a2+12​a​γ​ηx+ς3​μ​μx+ς2​μ​ηx​x+12​γ​μx​f)​d​x.\displaystyle\left.\hphantom{H_{2}=}{}-\varsigma_{2}af_{x}+\frac{1}{2}avf+\varsigma_{3}a^{2}+\frac{1}{2}a\gamma\eta_{x}+\varsigma_{3}\mu\mu_{x}+\varsigma_{2}\mu\eta_{xx}+\frac{1}{2}\gamma\mu_{x}f\right)dx.
Proof.

Direct computation gives

δ​H2δ​f=ς2​ax−ς1​fx​x+3​c12​f2−c2​f​fx​x−c22​fx2−c22​ηx​ηx​x−3​c18​η​ηx​x+12​a​v+12​γ​μx,\displaystyle\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta f}=\varsigma_{2}a_{x}-\varsigma_{1}f_{xx}+\frac{3c_{1}}{2}f^{2}-c_{2}ff_{xx}-\frac{c_{2}}{2}f_{x}^{2}-\frac{c_{2}}{2}\eta_{x}\eta_{xx}-\frac{3c_{1}}{8}\eta\eta_{xx}+\frac{1}{2}av+\frac{1}{2}\gamma\mu_{x},
δ​H2δ​η=3​c22​fx​ηx​x+c2​f​ηx​x​x+c22​fx​x​ηx−3​c14​f​ηx−3​c18​fx​η+ς1​ηx​x−ς2​μx​x+12​(a​γ)x,\displaystyle\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\eta}=\frac{3c_{2}}{2}f_{x}\eta_{xx}+c_{2}f\eta_{xxx}+\frac{c_{2}}{2}f_{xx}\eta_{x}-\frac{3c_{1}}{4}f\eta_{x}-\frac{3c_{1}}{8}f_{x}\eta+\varsigma_{1}\eta_{xx}-\varsigma_{2}\mu_{xx}+\frac{1}{2}(a\gamma)_{x},\!\! (3.4)
δ​H2δ​a=2​ς3​a+v​f+12​γ​ηx−ς2​fx,\displaystyle\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta a}=2\varsigma_{3}a+vf+\frac{1}{2}\gamma\eta_{x}-\varsigma_{2}f_{x},
δ​H2δ​μ=γx​f+12​γ​fx−12​v​ηx+ς2​ηx​x−2​ς3​μx.\displaystyle\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\mu}=\gamma_{x}f+\frac{1}{2}\gamma f_{x}-\frac{1}{2}v\eta_{x}+\varsigma_{2}\eta_{xx}-2\varsigma_{3}\mu_{x}.

Under the special freezing point

U^0=(c12​d​x2,0,0,0,(c2,0,c52))∈𝒢reg∗,\displaystyle\hat{U}_{0}=\left(\frac{c_{1}}{2}dx^{2},0,0,0,\left(c_{2},0,\frac{c_{5}}{2}\right)\right)\in\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*},

the system (3.1) reads

ut=c2​(δ​H2δ​u)x​x​x−c1​(δ​H2δ​u)x,vt=−c5​(δ​H2δ​v)x,\displaystyle u_{t}=c_{2}\left(\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta u}\right)_{xxx}-c_{1}\left(\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta u}\right)_{x},\qquad v_{t}=-c_{5}\left(\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta v}\right)_{x},
ψt=c14​δ​H2δ​ψ−c2​(δ​H2δ​ψ)x​x,γt=c5​δ​H2δ​γ.\displaystyle\psi_{t}=\frac{c_{1}}{4}\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\psi}-c_{2}\left(\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\psi}\right)_{xx},\qquad\gamma_{t}=c_{5}\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\gamma}. (3.5)

Using (3.2), we have

δ​H2δ​u=Λ−1​(δ​H2δ​f),δ​H2δ​ψ=Π−1​(δ​H2δ​η),c5​δ​H2δ​v=δ​H2δ​a,c5​δ​H2δ​γ=−δ​H2δ​μ.\displaystyle\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta u}=\Lambda^{-1}\left(\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta f}\right),\qquad\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\psi}=\Pi^{-1}\left(\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\eta}\right),\qquad c_{5}\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta v}=\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta a},\qquad c_{5}\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\gamma}=-\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\mu}.

The system (3.5) becomes

ut=−(δ​H2δ​f)x,ψt=−δ​H2δ​η,vt=−(δ​H2δ​a)x,γt=−δ​H2δ​μ,\displaystyle u_{t}=-\left(\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta f}\right)_{x},\qquad\psi_{t}=-\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\eta},\qquad v_{t}=-\left(\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta a}\right)_{x},\qquad\gamma_{t}=-\frac{\delta H_{2}}{\delta\mu},

which is the desired system (3.3) due to (3.2) and (3.4). We thus complete the proof of the theorem. ∎

3.3 Examples

Example 3.2 (an L2L^{2}-type metric M1,0,14,0,1,−1M_{1,0,\frac{1}{4},0,1,-1}).

The systems (3.3) reduces to

ft=ς1​fx​x​x−ς2​ax​x−3​f​fx+38​η​ηx​x−a​ax+12​μ​μx​x,\displaystyle f_{t}=\varsigma_{1}f_{xxx}-\varsigma_{2}a_{xx}-3ff_{x}+\frac{3}{8}\eta\eta_{xx}-aa_{x}+\frac{1}{2}\mu\mu_{xx},
ηt=4​ς1​ηx​x​x−3​f​ηx−32​fx​η−4​ς2​μx​x−2​(a​μ)x,\displaystyle\eta_{t}=4{\varsigma}_{1}\eta_{xxx}-3f\eta_{x}-\frac{3}{2}f_{x}\eta-4{\varsigma}_{2}\mu_{xx}-2(a\mu)_{x},
at=ς2​fx​x−2​ς3​ax−(a​f)x+12​(μ​ηx)x,\displaystyle a_{t}=\varsigma_{2}f_{xx}-2\varsigma_{3}a_{x}-(af)_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(\mu\eta_{x})_{x}, (3.6)
μt=ς2​ηx​x−2​ς3​μx−12​a​ηx−μx​f−12​μ​fx.\displaystyle\mu_{t}=\varsigma_{2}\eta_{xx}-2\varsigma_{3}\mu_{x}-\frac{1}{2}a\eta_{x}-\mu_{x}f-\frac{1}{2}\mu f_{x}.

We call this system (3.6) to be a Kuper-2KdV equation. Especially, (1) if we set η=μ=0\eta=\mu=0, we have

ft=ς1​fx​x​x−ς2​ax​x−3​f​fx−a​ax,at=ς2​fx​x−2​ς3​ax−(a​f)x,\displaystyle f_{t}=\varsigma_{1}f_{xxx}-\varsigma_{2}a_{xx}-3ff_{x}-aa_{x},\qquad a_{t}=\varsigma_{2}f_{xx}-2\varsigma_{3}a_{x}-(af)_{x},

which is a two-component generalization of the KdV equation with three parameters including the Ito equation in [17] for ς1≠0\varsigma_{1}\neq 0, ς2=ς3=0\varsigma_{2}=\varsigma_{3}=0; (2) if we set ς1=12\varsigma_{1}=\frac{1}{2}, ς2=0\varsigma_{2}=0, a=0a=0 and μ=0\mu=0, we have

ft=12​fx​x​x−3​f​fx+38​η​ηx​x,ηt=2​ηx​x​x−3​f​ηx−32​fx​η,\displaystyle f_{t}=\frac{1}{2}f_{xxx}-3ff_{x}+\frac{3}{8}\eta\eta_{xx},\qquad\eta_{t}=2\eta_{xxx}-3f\eta_{x}-\frac{3}{2}f_{x}\eta,

which is the Kuper–KdV equation in [23].

Let us remark that when we choose ς1=14\varsigma_{1}=\frac{1}{4} and ς2=ς3=0\varsigma_{2}=\varsigma_{3}=0, up to a rescaling, the Kuper–2KdV equation (3.6) is the super-Ito equation (equation (4.14b) in [1]) proposed by M. Antonowicz and A.P. Fordy, which has three Hamiltonian structures. According to our terminologies, we would like to call it the Kuper–Ito equation.

Example 3.3 (an H1H^{1}-type metric M1,1,14,1,1,−1M_{1,1,\frac{1}{4},1,1,-1}).

The systems (3.3) reduces to

ft−fx​x​t=ς1​fx​x​x−ς2​ax​x−3​f​fx+2​fx​fx​x+f​fx​x​x+38​η​ηx​x+12​ηx​ηx​x​x−a​ax+12​μ​μx​x,\displaystyle f_{t}-f_{xxt}=\varsigma_{1}f_{xxx}-\varsigma_{2}a_{xx}-3ff_{x}+2f_{x}f_{xx}+ff_{xxx}+\frac{3}{8}\eta\eta_{xx}+\frac{1}{2}\eta_{x}\eta_{xxx}-aa_{x}+\frac{1}{2}\mu\mu_{xx},
ηx​x​t−14​ηt=34​f​ηx+38​fx​η−f​ηx​x​x−12​fx​x​ηx−32​fx​ηx​x−ς1​ηx​x​x+ς2​μx​x−12​(a​μ)x,\displaystyle\eta_{xxt}-\frac{1}{4}\eta_{t}=\frac{3}{4}f\eta_{x}+\frac{3}{8}f_{x}\eta-f\eta_{xxx}-\frac{1}{2}f_{xx}\eta_{x}-\frac{3}{2}f_{x}\eta_{xx}-{\varsigma}_{1}\eta_{xxx}+{\varsigma}_{2}\mu_{xx}-\frac{1}{2}(a\mu)_{x}, (3.7)
at=ς2​fx​x−2​ς3​ax−(a​f)x+12​(μ​ηx)x,\displaystyle a_{t}=\varsigma_{2}f_{xx}-2\varsigma_{3}a_{x}-(af)_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(\mu\eta_{x})_{x},
μt=ς2​ηx​x−2​ς3​μx−12​a​ηx−μx​f−12​μ​fx.\displaystyle\mu_{t}=\varsigma_{2}\eta_{xx}-2\varsigma_{3}\mu_{x}-\frac{1}{2}a\eta_{x}-\mu_{x}f-\frac{1}{2}\mu f_{x}.

We call this system (3.7) to be a Kuper–2CH equation. Especially, (1) if we set ς1=ς2=ς3=0\varsigma_{1}=\varsigma_{2}=\varsigma_{3}=0 and η=μ=0\eta=\mu=0, we have

ft−fx​x​t=2​fx​fx​x+f​fx​x​x−3​f​fx−a​ax,at=−(a​f)x,\displaystyle f_{t}-f_{xxt}=2f_{x}f_{xx}+ff_{xxx}-3ff_{x}-aa_{x},\qquad a_{t}=-(af)_{x},

which is the 2-CH equation in [6, 13]; (2) if by setting ς1=ς2=ς3=0\varsigma_{1}=\varsigma_{2}=\varsigma_{3}=0, a=0a=0 and μ=0\mu=0, the system (3.7) becomes

ft−fx​x​t=f​fx​x​x+2​fx​fx​x−3​f​fx+38​η​ηx​x+12​ηx​ηx​x​x,\displaystyle f_{t}-f_{xxt}=ff_{xxx}+2f_{x}f_{xx}-3ff_{x}+\frac{3}{8}\eta\eta_{xx}+\frac{1}{2}\eta_{x}\eta_{xxx},
ηx​x​t−14​ηt=34​f​ηx+38​fx​η−f​ηx​x​x−12​fx​x​ηx−32​fx​ηx​x,\displaystyle\eta_{xxt}-\frac{1}{4}\eta_{t}=\frac{3}{4}f\eta_{x}+\frac{3}{8}f_{x}\eta-f\eta_{xxx}-\frac{1}{2}f_{xx}\eta_{x}-\frac{3}{2}f_{x}\eta_{xx},

which is the Kuper–CH equation in [10, 38].

4 Supersymmetric Euler equations on 𝓖𝐫𝐞𝐠∗\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*}}

In this section, we want to discuss a class of supersymmetric Euler equations on 𝒢∗\mathcal{G}^{*} associated to a special metric Mc1,c2,c1,c2,c5,−c5M_{c_{1},c_{2},c_{1},c_{2},c_{5},-c_{5}}. Moreover, we present a class of supersymmetric and bihamiltonian Euler equations.

4.1 Supersymmetric Euler equations on 𝓖𝐫𝐞𝐠∗\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*}} w.r.t. 𝑴𝒄𝟏,𝒄𝟐,𝒄𝟏,𝒄𝟐,𝒄𝟓,−𝒄𝟓\boldsymbol{M_{c_{1},c_{2},c_{1},c_{2},c_{5},-c_{5}}}

In this case, we have

c1=c3,c2=c4,c6=−c5.\displaystyle c_{1}=c_{3},\qquad c_{2}=c_{4},\qquad c_{6}=-c_{5}.

By setting ϕ=ηx\phi=\eta_{x} and α=μx\alpha=\mu_{x}, we obtain

u=c1​f−c2​fx​x,ψ=c2​ηx​x−c1​η,v=c5​a,γ=−c5​μ.\displaystyle u=c_{1}f-c_{2}f_{xx},\qquad\psi=c_{2}\eta_{xx}-c_{1}\eta,\qquad v=c_{5}a,\qquad\gamma=-c_{5}\mu.

Let us define a superderivative DD by D=∂θ+θ∂xD=\partial_{\theta}+\theta\partial_{x} and introduce two superfields

Φ=η+θ​f,Ω=μ+θ​a,\displaystyle\Phi=\eta+\theta f,\qquad\Omega=\mu+\theta a,

where θ\theta is an odd coordinate. A direct computation gives

Theorem 4.1.

The Euler equation (2.3) on 𝒢reg∗\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*} w.r.t. Mc1,c2,c1,c2,c5,−c5M_{c_{1},c_{2},c_{1},c_{2},c_{5},-c_{5}} is invariant under the supersymmetric transformation

δ​f=θ​ηx,δ​η=θ​f,δ​a=θ​μx,δ​μ=θ​a\displaystyle\delta f=\theta\eta_{x},\qquad\delta\eta=\theta f,\qquad\delta a=\theta\mu_{x},\qquad\delta\mu=\theta a

and could be rewritten as

4.2 Examples

Example 4.2 (another L2L^{2}-type metric M1,0,1,0,1,−1M_{1,0,1,0,1,-1}).

The system (4.1) reduces to

Φt=ς1​D6​Φ−32​(Φ​D3​Φ+D​Φ​D2​Φ)−ς2​D4​Ω+12​(D​Ω​D2​Ω+Ω​D3​Ω),\displaystyle\Phi_{t}=\varsigma_{1}D^{6}\Phi-\frac{3}{2}\big(\Phi D^{3}\Phi+D\Phi D^{2}\Phi\big)-\varsigma_{2}D^{4}\Omega+\frac{1}{2}\big(D\Omega D^{2}\Omega+\Omega D^{3}\Omega\big),
Ωt=ς2​D4​Φ−2​ς3​D2​Ω−12​(D​Ω​D2​Φ+2​D2​Ω​D​Φ+Ω​D3​Φ).\displaystyle\Omega_{t}=\varsigma_{2}D^{4}\Phi-2\varsigma_{3}D^{2}\Omega-\frac{1}{2}\big(D\Omega D^{2}\Phi+2D^{2}\Omega D\Phi+\Omega D^{3}\Phi\big). (4.2)

We call this system (4.2) to be a super-2KdV equation. Especially, (1) if we set η=μ=0\eta=\mu=0, we recover the two-component KdV equation again; (2) but if we choose ς1=12\varsigma_{1}=\frac{1}{2}, ς2=ς3=0\varsigma_{2}=\varsigma_{3}=0 and Ω=0\Omega=0, the system (4.2) becomes

Φt=12​D6​Φ−32​(Φ​D3​Φ+D​Φ​D2​Φ),\displaystyle\Phi_{t}=\frac{1}{2}D^{6}\Phi-\frac{3}{2}\big(\Phi D^{3}\Phi+D\Phi D^{2}\Phi\big),

equivalently in componentwise forms,

ft=12​fx​x​x−3​f​fx+32​η​ηx​x,ηt=12​ηx​x​x−32​(f​η)x,\displaystyle f_{t}=\frac{1}{2}f_{xxx}-3ff_{x}+\frac{3}{2}\eta\eta_{xx},\qquad\eta_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\eta_{xxx}-\frac{3}{2}(f\eta)_{x},

which is the super-KdV equation in [31].

Example 4.3 (another H1H^{1}-type metric M1,1,1,1,1,−1M_{1,1,1,1,1,-1}).

The system (4.1) reduces to

Φt−D4​Φt=ς1​D6​Φ−32​(Φ​D3​Φ+D​Φ​D2​Φ)+(D​Φ​D6​Φ+12​D2​Φ​D5​Φ+32​D3​Φ​D4​Φ)\displaystyle\Phi_{t}-D^{4}\Phi_{t}=\varsigma_{1}D^{6}\Phi-\frac{3}{2}(\Phi D^{3}\Phi+D\Phi D^{2}\Phi)+\left(D\Phi D^{6}\Phi+\frac{1}{2}D^{2}\Phi D^{5}\Phi+\frac{3}{2}D^{3}\Phi D^{4}\Phi\right)

Ωt=ς2​D4​Φ−2​ς3​D2​Ω−12​(D​Ω​D2​Φ+2​D2​Ω​D​Φ+Ω​D3​Φ).\displaystyle\Omega_{t}=\varsigma_{2}D^{4}\Phi-2\varsigma_{3}D^{2}\Omega-\frac{1}{2}\big(D\Omega D^{2}\Phi+2D^{2}\Omega D\Phi+\Omega D^{3}\Phi\big).

We call this system (4.3) to be a super-2CH equation. Especially, (1) if we set ς1=ς2=ς3=0\varsigma_{1}=\varsigma_{2}=\varsigma_{3}=0 and η=μ=0\eta=\mu=0, we obtain the 2-CH equation in [6, 13] again; (2) but if by setting ς1=ς2=ς3=0\varsigma_{1}=\varsigma_{2}=\varsigma_{3}=0 and Ω=0\Omega=0, the system (4.3) becomes

Φt−D4​Φt=(D​Φ​D6​Φ+12​D2​Φ​D5​Φ+32​D3​Φ​D4​Φ)−32​(Φ​D3​Φ+D​Φ​D2​Φ),\displaystyle\Phi_{t}-D^{4}\Phi_{t}=\left(D\Phi D^{6}\Phi+\frac{1}{2}D^{2}\Phi D^{5}\Phi+\frac{3}{2}D^{3}\Phi D^{4}\Phi\right)-\frac{3}{2}\big(\Phi D^{3}\Phi+D\Phi D^{2}\Phi\big),

which is the super-CH equation in [11].

w.r.t. 𝑴𝟎,𝒄𝟐,𝟎,𝒄𝟐,𝒄𝟓,−𝒄𝟓\boldsymbol{M_{0,c_{2},0,c_{2},c_{5},-c_{5}}} on 𝓖𝐫𝐞𝐠∗\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}_{\rm reg}^{*}}

Ωt=ς2​D4​Φ−2​ς3​D2​Ω−12​(D​Ω​D2​Φ+2​D2​Ω​D​Φ+Ω​D3​Φ).\displaystyle\Omega_{t}=\varsigma_{2}D^{4}\Phi-2\varsigma_{3}D^{2}\Omega-\frac{1}{2}\big(D\Omega D^{2}\Phi+2D^{2}\Omega D\Phi+\Omega D^{3}\Phi\big).

We call this system (4.4) to be a super-22HS equation. Especially, (i)(i) if we set ς1=ς2=ς3=0\varsigma_{1}=\varsigma_{2}=\varsigma_{3}=0 and η=μ=0\eta=\mu=0, we have

−fx​x​t=2​fx​fx​x+f​fx​x​x−a​ax,at=−(a​f)x,\displaystyle-f_{xxt}=2f_{x}f_{xx}+ff_{xxx}-aa_{x},\qquad a_{t}=-(af)_{x},

which is a 2-HS equation in [39]; (i​i)(ii) if by setting ς1=ς2=ς3=0\varsigma_{1}=\varsigma_{2}=\varsigma_{3}=0 and Ω=0\Omega=0, the system (4.4) becomes

−D4​Φt=D​Φ​D6​Φ+12​D2​Φ​D5​Φ+32​D3​Φ​D4​Φ,\displaystyle-D^{4}\Phi_{t}=D\Phi D^{6}\Phi+\frac{1}{2}D^{2}\Phi D^{5}\Phi+\frac{3}{2}D^{3}\Phi D^{4}\Phi,

which is the super-HS equation in [5, 24].

5 Concluding remarks

We have described Euler equations associated to the GNS algebra and shown that under which conditions there are superymmetric or bihamiltonian. Here we only obtain some sufficient conditions but not necessary conditions. As an application, we have naturally presented several generalizations of some well-known integrable systems including the Ito equation, the 2-CH equation and the 2-HS equation. It is well-known that the Virasoro algebra, the extended Virasoro algebra and the Neveu–Schwarz algebras are subalgebras of the GNS algebra. Thus our result could be regarded as a generalization of that related to those subalgebras, see for instances [2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 24, 25, 28, 30, 32, 33, 35, 37, 39] and references therein. In the past twenty years, in this subject it has grown in many different directions, please see [21] and references therein. Finally let us point out that in this paper all super-Hamiltonian operators are even. Recently, in [5, 26, 27], the classical Harry–Dym equation is supersymmetrized in two ways, either by even supersymmetric Hamiltonian operators or by odd supersymmetric Hamiltonian operators. Notice that the HS equation is one of a member of negative Harry–Dym hierarchy. It would be interesting to investigate whether the above point of view has an extension to the odd supersymmetric integrable system, for instance, the odd HS equation.
